title: I built and released an Android fishing puzzle game with Claude. Getting the tiny sprites right took a lot of iteration
author: ItzChiips
selftext:
I just released Fishdoku on Google Play. I’m the solo developer and used Claude heavily for the code and sprites, with ChatGPT helping with concept art and review.

The idea came from my wife. She loves logic puzzles, but solves them quickly enough that she was spending more time watching ads between rounds than playing. I wanted to make something she could keep playing without forced ads.

In Fishdoku, every bite opens a logic grid. Place one fish in each row, column and colored region, with no two touching, then reel in your catch. Around that is a collection of hundreds of fish across dozens of locations, with weather, time of day, shiny variants and legends to hunt.

**Google Play:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.fishdoku.game](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.fishdoku.game)

One part of the development that might interest people here is that the sprites are drawn in code. Refining a pet or angler meant changing the drawing code and checking it in the actual game.

At those sizes, a small change makes a big difference. A character could look fine enlarged but lose its shape on the dock. A glow could look nice at night but cover the face. An animated detail could technically be moving without being noticeable.

The most useful feedback ended up being very specific: separate the arm from the body, make the silhouette recognizable, shrink the glow, check it against both day and night backgrounds. I started working on one piece at a time and keeping notes on what was approved so later changes wouldn’t undo it.

I also learned to treat tests and visual review as separate jobs. Passing tests didn’t tell me whether a sprite was readable or whether playing through a feature felt good. That still took repeated play sessions and revisions.

It’s free with optional purchases and optional rewarded ads. No forced ads or energy timers, and there’s an untimed puzzle mode.

For others making games with AI, how are you handling visual consistency as the project grows? I’d be interested in how you keep new assets and revisions from drifting away from the rest of the game.
